title: Backend Overview & API Design
content:
1. API Request Processing Flow The browser sends an HTTPS request to https://<cloudfront-domain>/v1/.... CloudFront forwards requests matching /v1/* to API Gateway. API Gateway matches the corresponding Resource + Method; for Staff APIs, the Cognito User Pool Authorizer validates the token. API Gateway invokes Lambda using Lambda proxy integration. Lambda validates the request data and business permissions, accesses DynamoDB, and returns JSON with an HTTP status code. 2. Guest API Design Guests do not use Cognito. The session creation endpoint can be accessed without a token; the remaining Guest endpoints require a token issued by the backend.
Method Endpoint Lambda Function POST /v1/guest/sessions SecureTable-GuestServices Validate the table/bill and issue a Guest Session GET /v1/guest/menu SecureTable-GuestServices Return the list of dishes available for ordering POST /v1/guest/orders SecureTable-Ordering Place an order and reserve ingredients GET /v1/guest/orders SecureTable-Ordering View ordered items and their statuses in the current bill Example: Creating a session for table T01:
POST /v1/guest/sessions Content-Type: application/json { "table_id": "T01" } Lambda checks that the table is OCCUPIED and the bill is OPEN. If valid, the API returns a guest_session_token. When calling the order API, the frontend sends the token in the header:
Authorization: Bearer <guest_session_token> Content-Type: application/json Idempotency-Key: <unique-key-for-this-order> Example order request body (the dish ID must exist in SecureTable-MenuItems):
{ "items": [ { "dish_id": "D_BUN_BO_HUE", "qty": 2 } ] } After placing an order, guests can call GET /v1/guest/orders to view items with the statuses ORDERED, COMPLETED, or REJECTED, even after reloading the page. Guests do not have an endpoint for canceling orders.
Note: Lambda determines the bill_id from the Guest Session rather than accepting it as a user-supplied parameter. Guests can only read items belonging to the open bill associated with that session.
3. Staff API Design Staff members sign in through Cognito before calling endpoints under /v1/staff/*.
Method Endpoint Lambda Authorized Groups GET /v1/staff/tables SecureTable-Reception RECEPTION, ADMIN POST /v1/staff/bills SecureTable-Reception RECEPTION, ADMIN GET /v1/staff/bills SecureTable-Reception RECEPTION, ADMIN GET /v1/staff/bills/{billId} SecureTable-Reception RECEPTION, ADMIN GET /v1/staff/bills/{billId}/receipt SecureTable-Reception RECEPTION, ADMIN POST /v1/staff/bills/{billId}/close SecureTable-Reception RECEPTION, ADMIN GET /v1/staff/kitchen/queue SecureTable-Kitchen KITCHEN, ADMIN POST /v1/staff/kitchen/items/{itemId}/complete SecureTable-Kitchen KITCHEN, ADMIN POST /v1/staff/kitchen/items/{itemId}/reject SecureTable-Kitchen KITCHEN, ADMIN GET, POST /v1/staff/inventory/receipts SecureTable-Inventory INVENTORY, ADMIN GET, POST /v1/staff/inventory/receipts/{receiptId}/corrections SecureTable-Inventory INVENTORY, ADMIN GET /v1/staff/finance/daily/{date} SecureTable-AdminDashboard ADMIN GET /v1/staff/finance/summary SecureTable-AdminDashboard ADMIN GET /v1/staff/finance/weekly SecureTable-AdminDashboard ADMIN GET /v1/staff/audit-logs SecureTable-AdminDashboard ADMIN Note: This table shows the main routes found in SecureTable’s source code and deployment documentation. If your version of Inventory includes additional routes for reading ingredients, viewing receipt details, or making separate adjustments, create the exact Methods/Resources used by that frontend and Lambda version. Do not create routes solely because they appear in the original proposed API Spec.
Example: Opening a bill:
POST /v1/staff/bills Authorization: Bearer <staff_id_token> Content-Type: application/json Idempotency-Key: <unique-key-for-this-open-bill> { "table_id": "T01", "guest_count": 2 } API Gateway validates the Cognito ID Token. The Reception Lambda then checks the user’s group, guest_count, Idempotency-Key, and whether the table already has an open bill. If the table is occupied, the backend may return 409 Conflict.
4. Guest vs. Staff Authentication Item Guest Staff Cognito sign-in No Yes Token Guest Session Token Cognito ID Token Validation at API Gateway Authorization: NONE Cognito User Pool Authorizer Validation in Lambda Session expiration, correct table, and open bill sub, cognito:groups, and business permissions Access scope Menu, order placement, and items in the bill Based on staff group For SecureTable’s REST API and Cognito User Pool Authorizer, Staff Methods use an ID Token and leave Authorization Scopes empty. If scopes are required, API Gateway expects an access token containing the corresponding scopes, which does not match how the current frontend operates.
5. Data and Error Conventions Request/Response: JSON, Content-Type: application/json. Status codes: 200 for successful reads/updates, 201 for creation, 400 for invalid data, 401 for missing/invalid authentication, 403 for insufficient permissions, 409 for state conflicts, and 500 for server errors. Orders: Use an Idempotency-Key for POST /guest/orders to prevent duplicate orders if a customer retries after a network issue. DynamoDB: Operations affecting multiple tables use transactions/conditional writes to prevent inventory from being deducted or charges from being added twice. Security: Do not trust client-supplied role, bill_id, or table_id for operations requiring authorization checks; do not log tokens to CloudWatch Logs.

content:
Exploring the Shared Responsibility Model and Amazon S3 Data Security Published on: AWS Study Group VN Facebook Group Author: Thuy Nga Tasks Completed Studied official AWS documentation on the Shared Responsibility Model, focusing on customer security responsibilities when using Amazon EC2 and Amazon S3. Reviewed Amazon S3 security guidelines: Block Public Access, default SSE-S3 encryption, and S3 Versioning. Synthesized key takeaways into a practical security checklist and knowledge-sharing post. Key Findings & Outcomes Clearly distinguished AWS’s responsibility for protecting the underlying cloud infrastructure from the customer’s responsibility for governing data, access permissions, and workload configurations. Noted that new general-purpose S3 buckets enable all four Block Public Access settings by default, and newly uploaded objects are automatically encrypted at rest using SSE-S3. Understood that S3 Versioning is disabled by default; when enabled, it protects against accidental overwrites and deletions by preserving multiple object versions, though retained versions consume additional storage capacity. Lesson Learned Adopting a managed cloud service does not eliminate the customer’s responsibility to govern access permissions and protect data. Engineers must regularly audit access configurations and balance data recovery requirements against storage costs when enabling S3 Versioning.

title: System Overview & Architecture
content:
Before deploying services through the AWS Console, we need to understand how the components of SecureTable connect and exchange data. The system is built on an AWS Serverless architecture, focusing on three key requirements: supporting restaurant operations, protecting data, and optimizing costs for a small-scale deployment.
In this section, we will examine the architecture diagram used to deploy SecureTable, its main workflows, and the technologies selected for the project.
1. SecureTable Architecture Diagram 1.1. Guest Workflow Accessing the website: Customers scan the static QR code at their table. Their browser loads the interface through Amazon CloudFront, with the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files stored in Amazon S3. Creating a Guest Session: The frontend sends POST /v1/guest/sessions to Amazon API Gateway. The GuestServices Lambda checks in Amazon DynamoDB that the table is OCCUPIED and its associated bill is OPEN. If both conditions are met, the system issues a Guest Session Token. Viewing the menu: The frontend calls GET /v1/guest/menu with the token. GuestServices validates the session, retrieves menu items and ingredient availability from DynamoDB, and returns a list of dishes available for ordering. Placing an order: The frontend sends POST /v1/guest/orders to the Ordering Lambda. The function validates the session and order data, then performs DynamoDB Transactions to record the order and reserve the required ingredients. Order processing: Ordered items are stored in the system for the Kitchen team to process. Customers can place additional orders while their bill remains open. Customers do not sign in through Amazon Cognito. Access to Guest APIs is controlled by the Guest Session Token and the bill status checked by the backend.
1.2. Staff Workflow Signing in: Staff members access the Staff interface through CloudFront and authenticate using Amazon Cognito User Pool. Authorization: After signing in, staff members are redirected to the interface associated with their role. Staff APIs are protected by a Cognito Authorizer in API Gateway, with additional permission checks in Lambda. Reception: The Reception Lambda manages tables, opens bills, displays bill details, and closes bills. During bill closure, the system first changes the bill status to CLOSING before finalizing the process and releasing the table. Kitchen: The Kitchen Lambda retrieves pending items and allows staff to complete or reject them. Changes affecting inventory and bills are handled according to the business rules. Inventory: The Inventory Lambda records ingredient purchases, updates stock quantities, and stores adjustment history. Admin: The AdminDashboard Lambda provides financial data and activity records (Audit Logs) to support reviews of restaurant operations. Each Lambda accesses the required DynamoDB tables using its IAM Execution Role. Critical write operations use conditional updates, transactions, or Idempotency Keys to reduce conflicts and prevent duplicate processing.
1.3. Automated Reporting and Backup Reporting: Amazon EventBridge Scheduler invokes the Report Lambda on a schedule. The Lambda aggregates data from DynamoDB and sends reports to the administrator’s email through Amazon SNS. Backup: EventBridge Scheduler invokes the Backup Lambda. The Lambda initiates DynamoDB Export to S3 for the tables included in the backup scope. The data is stored in S3, and S3 Lifecycle can transition backup copies to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after the configured period. These two workflows operate independently of regular ordering requests. Data exports and storage-class transitions are asynchronous operations and do not provide instant recovery.
1.4. Monitoring, Security, and Reliability Amazon CloudWatch: Collects Lambda logs, metrics, and API Gateway monitoring data. CloudWatch Alarms can send alerts through SNS. AWS CloudTrail: Helps track AWS API activity at the account level. CloudTrail is separate from the business-level Audit Logs stored in DynamoDB. Amazon Cognito & AWS IAM: Authenticate staff and control access to AWS resources according to the principle of least privilege. Amazon CloudFront & HTTPS: Deliver the website over encrypted connections. AWS WAF provides additional request filtering on the CloudFront distribution. DynamoDB Transactions & Backup: Help maintain data consistency for critical operations and provide data for recovery in the event of a failure. Security limitation: Static QR codes can be copied. Guest Sessions are linked to open bills, so the current mechanism does not verify whether the person scanning the QR code is physically present at the table.
2. Technology Stack Component Technologies / Services Frontend HTML, CSS, JavaScript; Amazon S3, Amazon CloudFront Backend Python, AWS Lambda, Amazon API Gateway (REST API) Database Amazon DynamoDB Authentication & Authorization Amazon Cognito, AWS IAM, Guest Session Token Automation & Notifications Amazon EventBridge Scheduler, Amazon SNS Backup & Storage DynamoDB Export to S3, Amazon S3, S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval Monitoring & Security Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail; AWS WAF Deployment AWS Management Console 3. Reference Budget for the Demo Environment In the Proposal, we estimated the budget for a restaurant with 10 tables, approximately 20–30 bills per day, 40,000 REST API requests per month, 60,000 Lambda invocations per month, and approximately 1 GB of DynamoDB data, deployed in the Singapore Region (ap-southeast-1).
3.1. Estimated Costs for the Demo Configuration No. Service / Cost Category Estimated Cost (USD/month) 1 Amazon CloudFront & S3 Frontend $0.50 2 Amazon API Gateway (REST) $0.20 3 AWS Lambda $0.30 4 Amazon DynamoDB $1.00 5 Amazon Cognito $0.00 6 Amazon CloudWatch $1.00 7 Amazon EventBridge Scheduler & SNS $0.10 8 AWS WAF (included in the CloudFront Free Plan) $0.00 9 DynamoDB PITR, Export & S3 Backup $2.50 10 AWS CloudTrail Event History $0.00 Total Service Cost $5.60 Contingency Allowance $2.00 Total Estimated Budget $7.60/month Note: The $0 WAF estimate applies only if the distribution uses the CloudFront Free Plan and WAF is included in the plan. Lambda, PITR, export, and storage costs depend on the actual configuration and data volume.
3.2. Cost Optimization Measures Implemented Adopted a Serverless architecture instead of maintaining a continuously running EC2 server. Organized Lambda functions by business capability; for example, Reception combines table and bill management. Adjusted Lambda Memory and Timeout based on CloudWatch metrics. Delivered the static frontend through CloudFront and S3 without a separate web server. Used S3 Lifecycle to manage long-term backup storage.

title: Blog 2
content:
AWS Shared Responsibility Model Published on: AWS Study Group VN Facebook Group Author: Thuy Nga When adopting AWS, a common misconception is assuming that “moving to the cloud” means AWS handles 100% of security. In reality, security is a shared responsibility between AWS and the customer. The exact scope of customer responsibility depends on the specific AWS services selected and how workloads are configured.
AWS is responsible for “Security of the Cloud”: protecting the global infrastructure that runs all AWS services, including hardware, software, networking, and physical facilities. Customers are responsible for “Security in the Cloud”: protecting customer data, identities, access permissions, and service configurations under customer control.
Responsibilities Shift by Service Model With Amazon EC2 (IaaS): Customers must manage the guest operating system, security patches, installed application software, and Security Group firewall rules. AWS secures the underlying physical hosts and hypervisor, but does not patch or manage guest OS instances on the customer’s behalf. With Managed Services like Amazon S3: AWS operates the infrastructure layer, storage operating system, and service platform. Customers remain responsible for data classification, encryption configuration choices, bucket policies, and IAM access permissions. System Design Security Checklist Inventory all AWS services used in your architecture and explicitly document which configuration layers belong to your team. For EC2 workloads, establish a schedule for OS patching, application updates, and Security Group audits. For Amazon S3 and storage services, review data classification, public access controls, and encryption settings. Conduct periodic configuration and permission reviews rather than assuming a managed service automatically handles your data security posture. Understanding the Shared Responsibility Model prevents critical security gaps such as unpatched guest operating systems, overly broad IAM permissions, or misconfigured firewall rules. AWS secures the cloud infrastructure; customers must actively secure their workloads and data.

title: Creating and Configuring AWS Lambda Functions
content:
In this section, we will deploy 8 AWS Lambda Functions for SecureTable using source code packages prepared on GitHub. Each function has a ZIP file containing its source code and a JSON file containing its corresponding IAM Policy. We will create each Lambda with the default Execution Role, then add the permissions required to access DynamoDB and other AWS services.
All Lambda functions will be created in Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1, using Python 3.15 (python3.15) for Lambda Event Functions.
1. Prepare the Source Code on GitHub The source code has already been packaged in the SecureTable repository. Use the link below to download it before deployment:
Get the source code here
The Lambda directory has the following structure:
Lambda/ ├── GuestServices/ │ ├── SecureTable-GuestServices.zip │ └── SecureTable-GuestServices.json ├── Ordering/ │ ├── SecureTable-Ordering.zip │ └── SecureTable-Ordering.json ├── Reception/ │ ├── SecureTable-Reception.zip │ └── SecureTable-Reception.json ├── Kitchen/ │ ├── SecureTable-Kitchen.zip │ └── SecureTable-Kitchen.json ├── Inventory/ │ ├── SecureTable-Inventory.zip │ └── SecureTable-Inventory.json ├── AdminDashboard/ │ ├── SecureTable-AdminDashboard.zip │ └── SecureTable-AdminDashboard.json ├── Report/ │ ├── SecureTable-Report.zip │ └── SecureTable-Report.json └── Backup/ ├── SecureTable-Backup.zip └── SecureTable-Backup.json In each directory:
The .zip file contains the source code package to upload to AWS Lambda. The .json file contains the IAM Policy used to grant permissions to that Lambda function’s Execution Role. You can download the entire repository by selecting Code → Download ZIP on GitHub, then extract the repository to locate the files in the Lambda directory. Do not upload the ZIP file of the entire repository to Lambda; use only the corresponding SecureTable-<FunctionName>.zip file.
Note: The IAM Policy files on GitHub are configuration templates. Before using them, replace <YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID> with the AWS Account ID of the account where you are deploying. Other placeholders, such as <YOUR_BACKUP_BUCKET>, must also be replaced with actual values if they appear in a policy.
2. Create an AWS Lambda Function We will use SecureTable-GuestServices as an example. The remaining Lambda functions can be created in the same way.
Open AWS Lambda → Functions → Create function in the AWS Console.
Select Event Function if the interface asks you to choose a function type, then select Author from scratch.
Enter the following settings:
Setting Value Function name SecureTable-GuestServices Runtime Python 3.15 Architecture x86_64 Execution role Create a new role with basic Lambda permissions Select Create function.
Wait for AWS to create the function and open its details page.
Note: When you select Create a new role with basic Lambda permissions, AWS automatically creates an IAM Execution Role and grants permissions to write logs to Amazon CloudWatch (through AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole). Therefore, you do not need to create an IAM Role manually before creating the Lambda function. This role does not yet have permissions to access DynamoDB, S3, or SNS; we will add them in Section 4.
3. Upload Source Code to Lambda In the repository, open the Lambda/GuestServices directory.
Download SecureTable-GuestServices.zip to your computer.
Return to the SecureTable-GuestServices function in AWS Lambda and open the Code tab.
Select Upload from → .zip file, choose the downloaded file, and confirm with Save.
Under Runtime settings, verify that the Handler is set to:
lambda_function.lambda_handler If the Handler is incorrect, select Edit, enter the value above, and save the changes.
A typical ZIP package contains the main handler file, lambda_function.py, at its root. Some functions may include additional Python modules; for example, AdminDashboard uses modules for Finance and Audit Logs.
Note: Upload the complete ZIP file for each Lambda function. Do not extract it and upload individual files through the Console. Verify that lambda_function.py and any imported modules are placed correctly inside the ZIP package. Packages containing external libraries or code built for an older runtime should be tested for compatibility with Python 3.15.
4. Grant IAM Permissions to the Default Execution Role After creating the Lambda function, AWS provides permissions for writing CloudWatch Logs but does not grant access to business data. We will use the corresponding JSON file on GitHub to create an Inline Policy for each function.
4.1. Prepare the IAM Policy For SecureTable-GuestServices:
Open Lambda/GuestServices/SecureTable-GuestServices.json on GitHub. Copy the entire JSON content. Find and replace every occurrence of <YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID> with the 12-digit AWS Account ID of the account you are using. Verify that the DynamoDB table names and Region in the policy match the resources created in Section 5.4. For example, a sample ARN:
arn:aws:dynamodb:ap-southeast-1:<YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID>:table/SecureTable-Bills After replacing the placeholder, the ARN must contain the actual Account ID. IAM does not automatically replace <YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID> when the policy is saved.
For SecureTable-Backup.json, also replace <YOUR_BACKUP_BUCKET> with the name of the S3 bucket used for backups. For SecureTable-Report.json, verify the ARN of the SNS Topic SecureTable-FinancialReports. These resources will be created and configured in Section 5.7.
4.2. Attach an Inline Policy to the Execution Role Open AWS Lambda → Functions → SecureTable-GuestServices. Select Configuration → Permissions. Under Execution role, click the role name to open the IAM Console. Select Add permissions → Create inline policy. Switch to the JSON tab and paste the contents of SecureTable-GuestServices.json after replacing the Account ID. Select Next and enter a policy name, such as SecureTable-GuestServices-Policy. Select Create policy and verify that the new policy appears among the role’s permissions. Note: Attach only the JSON file corresponding to each function to that function’s Execution Role. Do not attach AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess to every Lambda function. The AWSLambdaDynamoDBExecutionRole policy is primarily intended for reading DynamoDB Streams and does not replace the table read/write permissions specified in SecureTable’s JSON files.
5. Configure Memory, Timeout, and Environment Variables Return to the Lambda function page and select Configuration → General configuration → Edit. Adjust Memory and Timeout according to the function’s requirements, then select Save. If the source code requires environment variables, open Configuration → Environment variables → Edit and enter the appropriate values. Confirm that the Runtime is Python 3.15 and the Handler is lambda_function.lambda_handler. The following table provides suggested initial settings for a demo environment; verify and adjust them during deployment:
Lambda Function Suggested Memory Suggested Timeout SecureTable-GuestServices 256 MB 15 seconds SecureTable-Ordering 256 MB 15 seconds SecureTable-Reception 512 MB 30 seconds SecureTable-Kitchen 256 MB 15 seconds SecureTable-Inventory 512 MB 30 seconds SecureTable-AdminDashboard 512 MB 30 seconds SecureTable-Report Depends on the task Configure in Section 5.7 SecureTable-Backup Depends on the task Configure in Section 5.7 Note: Memory and Timeout are not defined by the IAM Policy file. If a Lambda function reports a Task timed out error or runs out of memory, check CloudWatch Logs and adjust the configuration accordingly. For synchronous APIs, also consider the timeout limits of API Gateway.
6. Deploy the Remaining Lambda Functions Repeat the process of Create function → Upload ZIP → Configure → Create IAM Inline Policy for all 8 Lambda functions:
Lambda Function Source Code File IAM Policy File Function SecureTable-GuestServices SecureTable-GuestServices.zip SecureTable-GuestServices.json Issue Guest Sessions and retrieve the menu SecureTable-Ordering SecureTable-Ordering.zip SecureTable-Ordering.json Place orders, reserve ingredients, and view ordered items SecureTable-Reception SecureTable-Reception.zip SecureTable-Reception.json Manage tables and open or close bills SecureTable-Kitchen SecureTable-Kitchen.zip SecureTable-Kitchen.json Manage the kitchen queue and complete or reject items SecureTable-Inventory SecureTable-Inventory.zip SecureTable-Inventory.json Record stock receipts, conduct inventory counts, and correct receipts SecureTable-AdminDashboard SecureTable-AdminDashboard.zip SecureTable-AdminDashboard.json View the Finance Dashboard and Audit Logs SecureTable-Report SecureTable-Report.zip SecureTable-Report.json Generate reports and send them through SNS SecureTable-Backup SecureTable-Backup.zip SecureTable-Backup.json Initiate DynamoDB Export to S3 The SecureTable-Report and SecureTable-Backup functions do not need API Gateway integration. title: Proposal
content:
SecureTable – Restaurant Management System on AWS An Ingredient Management and QR Code Ordering System Built on AWS Serverless 1. Project Overview SecureTable is a restaurant management system designed for small-scale restaurants, focusing on food ordering, ingredient management, billing, and revenue tracking. Customers scan a fixed QR code at their table to view the menu and place orders, while staff use dedicated interfaces to carry out their tasks.
The system follows a serverless architecture on AWS to reduce server administration and facilitate future scaling. The project is deployed for testing in the AWS Asia Pacific (Singapore) Region – ap-southeast-1.
User roles:
Guest: Scan a QR code, view the menu, and place orders without creating an account. Reception: Manage tables and open or close bills. Kitchen: Mark dishes as completed or reject them. Inventory: Record stock receipts, update inventory, and adjust ingredient quantities. Admin: View financial reports and activity logs. 2. Project Objectives Build an AWS-hosted restaurant management website. Synchronize data across ordering, kitchen operations, inventory, and billing. Track ingredients received, reserved, consumed, and lost. Implement staff access control and log important actions for traceability. Automate reporting, backups, and system monitoring. Apply AWS Well-Architected principles for security, reliability, performance, operations, and cost optimization. 3. Problem Statement In many small restaurants, ingredient records, order taking, and revenue reporting still rely on notebooks or separate tools. This can lead to inaccurate inventory figures, delays in passing orders to the kitchen, and difficulty tracking changes to data.
Proposed solution: SecureTable uses a centralized data system. When a customer places an order, the order information is sent to the kitchen and linked to reserved ingredient quantities. As dishes are processed and bills are closed, inventory and financial records are updated according to business rules. Managers can review reports and audit logs instead of manually reconciling records.
4. Solution Architecture AWS Service Role Amazon S3 + Amazon CloudFront Store and deliver the web interface over HTTPS. Amazon API Gateway Receive and route API requests. AWS Lambda Handle GuestServices, Ordering, Reception, Kitchen, Inventory, AdminDashboard, Report, and Backup. Amazon DynamoDB Store table, bill, order, ingredient, financial, and audit data. Amazon Cognito + AWS IAM Authenticate staff and restrict access to AWS resources. Amazon EventBridge Scheduler + Amazon SNS Schedule reports and backups and send email notifications. Amazon CloudWatch + AWS CloudTrail Monitor, alert, and track activity across AWS. AWS WAF Filter certain types of abnormal web requests (if enabled in the deployment). Main workflows:
Guest: Scan QR code → CloudFront → API Gateway → GuestServices/Ordering → DynamoDB. A guest session is valid only while its associated bill is open. Staff: Sign in through Cognito → Call API Gateway → Business-specific Lambda → DynamoDB. Kitchen/Inventory: Process dishes or ingredients; use conditional updates and transactions when needed to maintain data consistency. Automation: EventBridge Scheduler → Report/Backup Lambda → SNS, or export DynamoDB data to S3. Well-Architected approach: Apply least-privilege IAM, HTTPS, and Cognito for security; DynamoDB transactions and backups for reliability; CloudWatch for operations; Lambda and DynamoDB for on-demand scalability; and resource usage monitoring for cost optimization.
5. Implementation Timeline Phase Activities Weeks 1–2 Analyze requirements and design the architecture and DynamoDB data model. Weeks 3–4 Deploy the S3/CloudFront frontend, Cognito, API Gateway, and core Lambda functions. Weeks 5–6 Complete Ordering, Kitchen, Inventory, Reception, Finance/Audit, and reporting features. Weeks 7–8 Add monitoring, security, and backups; test the system and prepare the demo and Workshop documentation. 6. Estimated Budget The budget covers one month of testing and demonstration in the AWS Singapore Region (ap-southeast-1), assuming a serverless architecture and low traffic. The amounts below are planning estimates, not actual invoices or figures verified through AWS Pricing Calculator.
6.1. Budget Assumptions Parameter Assumption Restaurant size 10 tables, approximately 20–30 bills per day API traffic Approximately 40,000 REST API requests per month Backend processing Approximately 60,000 Lambda invocations per month, mostly at 256 MB Data Approximately 1 GB in DynamoDB Reporting and backups Scheduled reports; backups of approximately 13 tables each week CloudFront & WAF Assumes the CloudFront Free Plan, with WAF included in the plan 6.2. Estimated Monthly Costs No. AWS Service Basis of Estimate Cost (USD/month) 1 Amazon CloudFront & S3 Static frontend; Free Plan, with an allowance for S3 storage/requests outside the plan $0.50 2 Amazon API Gateway (REST) 40,000 requests/month $0.20 3 AWS Lambda 60,000 invocations/month, mostly at 256 MB $0.30 4 Amazon DynamoDB Approximately 1 GB of data and low read/write traffic $1.00 5 Amazon Cognito Small number of staff accounts, assumed eligible for free usage $0.00 6 Amazon CloudWatch Low-volume logs and several standard alarms $1.00 7 EventBridge Scheduler & SNS Report/backup schedules and notification emails $0.10 8 AWS WAF Assumed to be included in the CloudFront Free Plan $0.00 9 DynamoDB PITR, Export & S3 Backup Allowance for PITR, weekly exports, and backup storage $2.50 10 AWS CloudTrail Default Event History only $0.00 Total estimated service cost $5.60 Contingency allowance $2.00 Total estimated budget $7.60/month Total estimated budget for 12 months: $91.20, assuming the same configuration and usage levels are maintained. Actual costs may vary depending on usage, individual table sizes, AWS Free Tier/credits, and additional enabled features. If AWS WAF is billed separately, its charges must be added.
Reference: AWS Pricing Calculator.
7. Risks and Mitigation Measures Risk Mitigation A static QR code is copied and used to place orders remotely Restrict sessions to open bills; allow Reception to review disputed orders. Additional authentication is a possible future improvement. Concurrent orders cause inventory inconsistencies Use DynamoDB transactions, conditional updates, and idempotency for critical operations. Lambda/API errors or timeouts Monitor with CloudWatch, configure alerts, and allow safe retries for operations designed to support them. Unauthorized access or excessive permissions Use Cognito for staff, least-privilege IAM, and backend authorization checks. Data loss or budget overruns Perform scheduled backups, test recovery, use AWS Budgets, and review resources regularly. 8. Expected Outcomes SecureTable aims to deliver an MVP that demonstrates the complete workflow: Reception opens a table → a customer scans the QR code and places an order → Kitchen processes the order → Inventory updates ingredient quantities → Reception closes the bill → Admin reviews reports and activity logs.
From a technical perspective, the project should demonstrate that AWS services work together as shown in the architecture diagram, business data is updated consistently, access is controlled, and monitoring, reporting, and backup capabilities are in place. In the long term, the system could be expanded to support online payments, multiple branches, and stronger QR code verification mechanisms.

title: Blog 3
content:
AWS Security: Starting with Identity and Access Control Published on: AWS Study Group VN Facebook Group Author: Thuy Nga When building systems on AWS, security goes beyond firewalls and private networks. You must strictly govern which identities can access resources, what actions they are permitted to perform, and under which conditions. The AWS Well-Architected Security Pillar recommends establishing layered identity controls across design, deployment, and operations.
1. Protect the Root User The AWS account Root user holds unrestricted access to all resources in the account. AWS strongly recommends using the Root user only for tasks that explicitly require root privileges, and never creating programmatic access keys for the Root user. Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) must be enforced on the Root user across all AWS account types.
2. Use Appropriate Identities and Temporary Credentials For human users within an organization, AWS recommends identity federation with short-lived credentials; AWS IAM Identity Center provides centralized multi-account access management. For applications and compute workloads running on AWS, always use IAM Roles to provide temporary credentials.
Temporary credentials automatically expire after a defined lifetime, after which AWS rejects them for new API requests. This eliminates the risk of distributing or embedding long-term static credentials in application code.
3. Grant Only the Permissions Workloads Actually Need (Least Privilege) The Principle of Least Privilege means granting only the minimum permissions required to complete a specific task, scoped by actions, resources, and conditions.
For example, if an application only needs to read objects whose keys start with reports/, the IAM policy should scope s3:GetObject strictly to that prefix (arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket/reports/*). In Amazon S3, “folders” shown in the console are actually object key prefixes rather than physical directories. If the workload also needs to list objects under that prefix, s3:ListBucket must be granted separately on the bucket ARN with a s3:prefix condition.
4. Audit Account Activity with AWS CloudTrail CloudTrail Event History provides a 90-day searchable record of management events per AWS Region. By default, Event History displays only management events-it does not include data events, CloudTrail Insights events, or network activity events. For long-term retention, multi-region auditing, and data event visibility, configure a dedicated CloudTrail Trail or CloudTrail Lake Event Data Store.
Getting Started Checklist Enable MFA for the Root user and stop using Root for everyday administrative tasks. Prefer identity federation, IAM Roles, and temporary credentials over static IAM access keys. Scope IAM policies tightly by specific actions, resource ARNs, and conditions. Verify event scope coverage when investigating activity in AWS CloudTrail. Cloud security requires continuous review: regularly verify which identities hold permissions, whether those permissions remain necessary, and whether account activity is being logged at the required depth.
References AWS Well-Architected Framework – Security Pillar Best practices to protect your AWS account root user Security best practices in IAM AWS security credentials Viewing recent management events with the CloudTrail console #AWS #CloudSecurity #IAM

title: Frontend Deployment
content:
In this section, we will deploy the SecureTable frontend to Amazon S3 and deliver the website through Amazon CloudFront. The system uses a single private S3 bucket to store the Guest and Staff pages, with CloudFront providing access over HTTPS.
1. Create an S3 Bucket Open Amazon S3 in the AWS Console and select Create bucket. Select AWS Region: Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1. Enter a bucket name. Keep Object Ownership: ACLs disabled and enable Block all public access. Leave the remaining settings at their defaults, then select Create bucket. Note: You do not need to enable S3 Static Website Hosting or make the bucket public. CloudFront accesses the content through Origin Access Control (OAC).
2. Upload the Frontend Open the newly created bucket and select Upload. Upload the SecureTable frontend source code available here. Select Upload to complete the process. Place index.html in the bucket root directory so CloudFront can load the default page.
Note: The paths in the HTML files must match the actual file locations in S3. S3 hosts only static content; staff authentication and order processing will be implemented in later sections.
3. Create a CloudFront Distribution Open Amazon CloudFront and select Create distribution. Select the CloudFront Free Plan for the distribution and enable AWS WAF within the plan’s included features. Choose Amazon S3 as the origin, then select the frontend bucket you created. Use Origin Access Control (OAC) with Sign requests (recommended) to allow CloudFront to read from the private bucket. Leave Origin path empty because the frontend files are located in the bucket root directory. Create the distribution and verify that the S3 bucket policy grants CloudFront read access. If the Console does not update the policy automatically, apply the bucket policy provided by CloudFront. After creation, set the Default root object to index.html. Save the changes and check that the distribution status becomes Deployed. CloudFront provides a domain name in the format dxxxxxxxxxxxxx.cloudfront.net. This is the address used to access SecureTable during the workshop.
Notes:
The six-month AWS Free Plan and the CloudFront Free Plan are separate programs. Verify that the distribution is using the CloudFront Free Plan to keep the included features within the free usage limits. AWS WAF has been enabled for CloudFront. Its configuration and monitoring will be covered in 5.8 – Security Hardening & System Monitoring. If you cannot create a distribution because your account requires verification, follow 5.2 – Prerequisites.

title: Integrating Lambda with Amazon API Gateway
content:
In this section, we will create a REST API, configure its Resources and Methods, set up a Cognito Authorizer, connect API Gateway to CloudFront, and then test the main features.
1. Create a REST API in Amazon API Gateway Open Amazon API Gateway in the AWS Console and select the Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1 Region.
Select APIs → Create API.
Under REST API, choose Build.
Select New API and enter the following settings:
Setting Value API name SecureTable-API API type REST API Endpoint Type Regional Select Create API, then open Resources.
Note: SecureTable uses a REST API, not an HTTP API. All Lambda functions were created in ap-southeast-1 in the previous section. The endpoints will begin with the /v1 resource, while the deployment stage will be dev.
2. Create Resources and Methods for Guests We will use POST /v1/guest/sessions as an example:
Under Resources, select the root resource / → Create resource. Create a v1 resource, then create guest under /v1, followed by sessions under /v1/guest. Select /v1/guest/sessions → Create method → choose POST as the HTTP method. Configure the integration as follows: Integration type: Lambda function. Lambda proxy integration: Enabled. Lambda function: SecureTable-GuestServices. Region: ap-southeast-1. Under Method request / Authorization, select NONE. Save the method and approve the permission for API Gateway to invoke Lambda if the Console displays a confirmation prompt. Continue creating the remaining Guest endpoints:
Method Resource Lambda integration Authorization POST /v1/guest/sessions SecureTable-GuestServices NONE GET /v1/guest/menu SecureTable-GuestServices NONE POST /v1/guest/orders SecureTable-Ordering NONE GET /v1/guest/orders SecureTable-Ordering NONE Note: Authorization: NONE only means that API Gateway does not use a Cognito Authorizer for these methods. POST /guest/sessions still requires the table to have an open bill; the other Guest APIs require Authorization: Bearer <guest_session_token>, which is validated by Lambda. In particular, GET /guest/orders only returns items belonging to the open bill associated with the Guest Session; it does not use a bill_id provided by the customer.
3. Create a Cognito User Pool Authorizer for Staff In SecureTable-API, open Authorizers → Create authorizer. Enter Authorizer name: SecureTableStaffAuthorizer. Select Authorizer type: Cognito / Cognito user pool (depending on the Console interface). Select the Cognito User Pool created for Staff in ap-southeast-1. Under Token source, enter Authorization. Select Create authorizer. When creating a Staff method, select SecureTableStaffAuthorizer under Method request → Authorization and leave Authorization Scopes empty.
Note: The SecureTable frontend sends a Cognito ID Token when calling Staff APIs. With a REST API Cognito User Pool Authorizer, leaving Authorization Scopes empty allows API Gateway to validate the ID Token. Lambda then checks cognito:groups to determine whether the user has the RECEPTION, KITCHEN, INVENTORY, or ADMIN role. Successfully signing in does not automatically grant access to every endpoint.
4. Integrate Staff APIs with Lambda Return to Resources and create a staff resource under /v1. Create child resources for each business function, such as bills, kitchen, inventory, and finance. Create the HTTP methods for each resource and enable Lambda proxy integration. Select the Lambda function according to the table below. For all Staff Methods, set Authorization: SecureTableStaffAuthorizer and leave Authorization Scopes empty. Method Resource Lambda integration GET /v1/staff/tables SecureTable-Reception GET, POST /v1/staff/bills SecureTable-Reception GET /v1/staff/bills/{billId} SecureTable-Reception GET /v1/staff/bills/{billId}/receipt SecureTable-Reception POST /v1/staff/bills/{billId}/close SecureTable-Reception GET /v1/staff/kitchen/queue SecureTable-Kitchen POST /v1/staff/kitchen/items/{itemId}/complete SecureTable-Kitchen POST /v1/staff/kitchen/items/{itemId}/reject SecureTable-Kitchen GET, POST /v1/staff/inventory/receipts SecureTable-Inventory GET, POST /v1/staff/inventory/receipts/{receiptId}/corrections SecureTable-Inventory GET /v1/staff/finance/daily/{date} SecureTable-AdminDashboard GET /v1/staff/finance/summary SecureTable-AdminDashboard GET /v1/staff/finance/weekly SecureTable-AdminDashboard GET /v1/staff/audit-logs SecureTable-AdminDashboard Notes:
When creating {billId}, {itemId}, {receiptId}, and {date}, preserve the curly braces and exact capitalization. These are Path Parameters passed to Lambda through pathParameters. For resources with multiple methods, such as /v1/staff/bills, create GET and POST separately, even if both invoke the same Lambda function. The table above lists the main endpoints in the SecureTable design. If the deployed Inventory version includes additional endpoints for viewing ingredients, receipt details, or inventory counts, create the corresponding Methods and Resources according to the actual Lambda code and frontend requests. Do not create routes that the Lambda does not implement. 5. Deploy the REST API to the dev Stage After creating the Resources, Methods, and Authorizer:
On the SecureTable-API page, select Deploy API. Under Stage, select New stage if this is the first deployment. Enter Stage name: dev, then confirm Deploy. Open Stages → dev and copy the Invoke URL. The Invoke URL has the following format:
https://<api-id>.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/dev For example, the full URL for calling the Guest Session API is:
https://<api-id>.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/dev/v1/guest/sessions Note: dev is the Stage, while v1 is a Resource. Every time you create or modify a Method, Integration, or Authorization setting in a REST API, you must deploy the API again to the dev stage for the changes to take effect. Otherwise, users may still be calling the previous API deployment.
6. Connect API Gateway to Amazon CloudFront In the source code, the frontend calls APIs using relative paths such as fetch('/v1/guest/menu'). Therefore, CloudFront must be configured to forward /v1/* requests to API Gateway.
6.1. Add an API Gateway Origin Open CloudFront → Distributions and select the distribution serving the SecureTable website.
Select Origins → Create origin.
Configure the following settings:
Setting Value Origin domain <api-id>.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com Origin path /dev Protocol HTTPS only Save the newly created Origin.
6.2. Create a CloudFront Behavior for the API In the same distribution, open Behaviors → Create behavior.
Apply the following settings:
Setting Value Path pattern /v1/* Origin The API Gateway Origin created above Viewer protocol policy Redirect HTTP to HTTPS Allowed HTTP methods GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, POST, PATCH, DELETE Cache policy CachingDisabled Origin request policy AllViewerExceptHostHeader Save the Behavior and confirm that the /v1/* behavior has the appropriate priority ahead of Default (*).
Verify that the Default behavior (*) still uses the S3 Origin with OAC to serve HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
When the frontend requests:
https://<cloudfront-domain>/v1/guest/menu CloudFront forwards the request to API Gateway at:
https://<api-id>.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/dev/v1/guest/menu Important notes:
Set the Origin path to /dev only, not /dev/v1. Because the browser already requests /v1/..., adding v1 to the Origin path would duplicate the path and could cause 403/404 errors. Do not include https:// in the Origin domain field. CachingDisabled prevents CloudFront from caching dynamic API responses. AllViewerExceptHostHeader forwards the necessary headers, including Authorization, while using the API Gateway Origin’s Host header. This configuration is suitable for API Gateway endpoints that use Bearer Tokens. Because the frontend and API share the same CloudFront domain, standard fetch('/v1/...') requests do not require separate CORS configuration. If the frontend later calls the execute-api domain directly, CORS must be configured appropriately. After completing these steps, the SecureTable frontend is connected to AWS Lambda through CloudFront and API Gateway, and the Staff APIs are authenticated through Cognito. In the next section, 5.7 – Automated Reporting & Data Backup, we will configure EventBridge Scheduler, Amazon SNS, and the process of exporting DynamoDB backups to Amazon S3.

title: Database Setup
content:
In this section, we will create Amazon DynamoDB tables to store table information, bills, orders, menu items, ingredients, and operational history for SecureTable. The tables are deployed in Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1, using On-demand capacity mode to accommodate demo traffic.
1. Create a DynamoDB Table We will create the SecureTable-Tables table:
Open Amazon DynamoDB in the AWS Console and select Tables → Create table. Enter Table name: SecureTable-Tables. Enter Partition key: table_id with the String data type. Leave Sort key empty. Keep Default settings (Capacity mode defaults to On-demand). Select Create table and wait until the table status changes to Active. Note: The Partition key and Sort key must match the names and data types used by the Lambda functions. Do not arbitrarily change table_id to id, as the backend would then be unable to retrieve the data.
2. Create the Remaining Tables Repeat the steps above to create the remaining SecureTable tables. The following primary keys are based on the deployed data structure and source code:
DynamoDB Table Partition key Sort key SecureTable-Tables table_id - SecureTable-Bills bill_id - SecureTable-Orders order_id - SecureTable-OrderItems item_id - SecureTable-MenuItems dish_id - SecureTable-Ingredients ingredient_id - SecureTable-InventoryReceipts receipt_id - SecureTable-InventoryCorrections receipt_id correction_id SecureTable-ReceiptCorrectionState receipt_id - SecureTable-InventoryMovements movement_id - SecureTable-InventoryCounts count_id - SecureTable-FinanceLedger entry_id - SecureTable-AuditLogs audit_id - SecureTable-GuestSessions session_hash - SecureTable-Idempotency scope key SecureTable-PendingByIngredient ingredient_id item_id SecureTable-NotificationOutbox event_id - SecureTable-ReportDispatch report_key - All keys listed above use the String data type. The system also uses SecureTable-ReportDispatch to track report delivery status and SecureTable-NotificationOutbox for notification events. These supporting tables must be created with the keys expected by their corresponding Lambda functions before those features are enabled.
Notes:
SecureTable uses a total of 18 DynamoDB tables, configured with On-demand capacity mode. Of these, 13 business tables are included in the scheduled backup scope. The SecureTable-OrderItems table uses 2 Global Secondary Indexes (GSIs) to support queries. To create a GSI, navigate to DynamoDB → Tables → SecureTable-OrderItems → Indexes → Create index and configure it according to the system’s query keys. Wait until the GSI status changes to Active before using it. 3. Enable Time to Live (TTL) SecureTable uses TTL to automatically clean up temporary data.
Open the SecureTable-GuestSessions table. Under Additional settings, find Time to Live (TTL) and select Turn on. Enter TTL attribute name: expires_at, then save the changes. Repeat the process for the SecureTable-Idempotency table, using the ttl attribute. Note: TTL values must be Unix timestamps in seconds, and DynamoDB deletes expired items asynchronously rather than immediately. Therefore, Lambda must still check session expiration when processing requests.
4. Add Initial Data To allow Reception to open bills, table records must first be created in DynamoDB:
Open SecureTable-Tables → Explore table items. Select Create item. Add the following sample item: { "table_id": { "S": "T01" }, "name": { "S": "Bàn 01" }, "status": { "S": "FREE" } } Select Create item, then repeat for T02, T03, and so on, based on the number of tables in the restaurant. Add menu and ingredient data to SecureTable-MenuItems and SecureTable-Ingredients. Note: DynamoDB JSON uses a different syntax from regular JSON. Make sure to select the correct input mode in the Console. The dish_id and ingredient_id values referenced in the menu and recipes must match the corresponding ingredient data.
5. Verify the Results Navigate to DynamoDB → Tables and confirm that all created tables have the Active status. Open SecureTable-Tables → Explore table items and verify the records for T01, T02, and so on. Confirm that the tables use On-demand capacity mode. Verify that TTL is enabled for the session and idempotency tables. Note: Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) must be enabled for the 13 tables included in the export-to-S3 backup scope. We will configure and verify PITR in 5.7 – Automated Reporting & Data Backup. PITR incurs separate charges, even when no export job is running.
Once these steps are complete, the database is ready to be connected to Lambda in 5.6 – Backend Development with AWS Lambda & API Gateway.

title: Authentication & Authorization
content:
In this section, we will configure an Amazon Cognito User Pool to authenticate staff members and assign permissions based on their roles in SecureTable.
Note: Customers (Guests) do not use Cognito. Guests receive a Session Token through an API when their table has an open bill.
1. Create a Cognito User Pool Open Amazon Cognito in the AWS Console and select Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1 as the Region. Select User pools → Create user pool. Select Single-page application (SPA) as the application type for the HTML/JavaScript frontend. Name the User Pool, for example SecureTable-Staff, and use Username and password for sign-in. Disable Self-registration so that only administrators can create staff accounts, then complete Create user pool. Note: There is no need to create a User Pool for Guests.
2. Configure the App Client & Login Page In the User Pool, open App clients and create or select the App Client for the Staff website. Choose Single-page application (SPA) and do not use a Client Secret. Enable Authorization code grant with PKCE; select at least the openid OAuth scope (add email and profile if required by the interface). Configure the following URLs, replacing <cloudfront-domain> with the domain from Section 5.3: Callback URL: https://<cloudfront-domain>/callback.html Sign-out URL: https://<cloudfront-domain>/login.html Under Domain, create a Cognito domain and configure the User Pool’s login page (Managed login or Hosted UI). Save the configuration and record the User Pool ID, App Client ID, and Cognito domain. Note: The Callback URL must exactly match the website URL, including https:// and /callback.html. Do not include a Client Secret in frontend JavaScript.
3. Create Permission Groups & Staff Accounts In the User Pool, select Groups → Create group. Create the following groups: Cognito Group Function RECEPTION Manage tables and open or close bills KITCHEN Receive and process orders INVENTORY Record stock receipts and adjust ingredients ADMIN View financial reports and Audit Logs Select Users → Create user to create staff accounts. Add each staff member to the appropriate group under Group membership. Note: Cognito includes group information in the cognito:groups claim in the ID Token. Redirecting users based on their roles does not replace backend authorization checks. Staff APIs will be protected by a Cognito Authorizer, with additional permission checks in Lambda in Section 5.6.
4. Connect Cognito to the Frontend Open the SecureTable frontend’s config.js file. Update the Cognito configuration: window.SECURETABLE_CONFIG = Object.freeze({ cognitoDomain: 'https://<your-cognito-domain>', clientId: '<your-app-client-id>', userPoolId: '<your-user-pool-id>' }); Upload config.js to the frontend S3 bucket, overwriting the existing file. Create a CloudFront Invalidation for /config.js if the website still loads the old configuration. Open https://<cloudfront-domain>/login.html, sign in with a Staff account, and verify that the system redirects to callback.html and then to the correct interface for the user’s group. Note: At this stage, we are verifying login and interface redirection. Business APIs will become fully functional after the backend is deployed in Section 5.6.
After completing these steps, Cognito is configured for Staff, and the permission groups and staff accounts are ready.

title: Workshop
content:
Building the SecureTable Restaurant Management System with AWS Serverless Overview AWS Serverless enables developers to build and deploy applications without managing servers directly. Services such as AWS Lambda, Amazon API Gateway, and Amazon DynamoDB handle requests, store data, and scale according to demand, reducing operational overhead.
In this workshop, we will learn how to build and deploy SecureTable, a restaurant management system on AWS that focuses on ingredient inventory management, QR code ordering, order processing, bill management, and revenue tracking.
The system uses a Serverless architecture, combining AWS services to deliver the web interface, process business logic, authenticate users, store data, and monitor system operations.
The main components we will deploy include:
Frontend – Amazon S3 & Amazon CloudFront: Host and deliver web interfaces for customers and staff over HTTPS. Authentication – Amazon Cognito & AWS IAM: Authenticate staff, manage permissions, and control access to AWS resources. Backend – AWS Lambda & Amazon API Gateway: Build APIs for ordering, table and bill management, kitchen operations, inventory management, and reporting. Database – Amazon DynamoDB: Store restaurant data and use DynamoDB Transactions for operations that require data consistency. Automation – Amazon EventBridge Scheduler & Amazon SNS: Schedule reports and data backups, and send email notifications. Monitoring & Security – Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail & AWS WAF: Monitor the system, record AWS activity, and provide additional web protection when WAF is enabled. By the end of this workshop, we will have a working SecureTable system deployed on AWS: customers can scan QR codes to place orders, staff can manage restaurant operations, and administrators can view operational data.
The workshop also covers testing, monitoring, and resource optimization based on the principles of the AWS Well-Architected Framework.
Contents System Overview & Architecture Prerequisites Frontend Deployment Database Setup Authentication & Authorization Backend Development Automated Reporting & Data Backup Security Hardening & System Monitoring End-to-End System Testing Resource Cleanup

title: Backend Development
content:
The system uses a Serverless architecture: there is no need to manage EC2 instances or continuously running web servers. Lambda functions are invoked when API requests arrive or scheduled events occur.
1. Backend Processing Architecture There are two main workflows:
Guest: Customer scans a QR code → CloudFront → API Gateway → GuestServices/Ordering Lambda → DynamoDB. Guests do not sign in through Cognito; the Lambda functions validate the Guest Session Token and the bill status. Staff: Staff sign in through Cognito → CloudFront → API Gateway (Cognito Authorizer) → Corresponding Lambda → DynamoDB. In addition to authentication, the Lambda functions check whether the user belongs to the RECEPTION, KITCHEN, INVENTORY, or ADMIN group. Requests from the frontend use paths under /v1/*. In CloudFront, these requests are routed to the API Gateway REST API instead of S3.
2. SecureTable Lambda Functions After consolidating functions that handle related business operations, SecureTable organizes its backend into 8 Lambda functions:
Lambda Main Responsibility Trigger SecureTable-GuestServices Issue Guest Sessions and return the menu API Gateway – Guest SecureTable-Ordering Receive orders, reserve ingredients, and retrieve previously ordered items API Gateway – Guest SecureTable-Reception View tables, open/close bills, and view bill details API Gateway – Staff SecureTable-Kitchen View the kitchen queue, complete or reject ordered items API Gateway – Staff SecureTable-Inventory Record stock receipts, view receipt records, and adjust inventory API Gateway – Staff SecureTable-AdminDashboard Aggregate financial data and query Audit Logs API Gateway – Staff SecureTable-Report Generate and send scheduled reports EventBridge Scheduler SecureTable-Backup Initiate DynamoDB backups to S3 EventBridge Scheduler Note: Report and Backup do not require public API endpoints. EventBridge schedules, SNS configuration, and S3 backups will be covered in 5.7 – Automated Reporting & Data Backup.
3. Deployment Order We will proceed through three sections:
5.6.1 – Backend Overview & API Design: Identify the endpoints required by Guests and Staff, their HTTP methods, and the Lambda functions that handle them. 5.6.2 – Creating and Configuring AWS Lambda Functions: Create functions, upload source code, configure runtimes, and assign IAM Execution Roles. 5.6.3 – Integrating Lambda with Amazon API Gateway: Create a REST API, configure Lambda proxy integration, enable the Cognito Authorizer, and configure CloudFront so the frontend can call the API. Note: DynamoDB tables must be created with the correct names and keys in Section 5.4 before testing the Lambda functions. In addition, the frontend can call the API only after API Gateway has been deployed and the /v1/* CloudFront behavior has been configured correctly.

title: Automated Reporting & Data Backup
content:
In this section, we will use Amazon EventBridge Scheduler to automatically send financial reports and back up SecureTable data.
SecureTable uses two automated workflows:
Reporting: EventBridge Scheduler → SecureTable-Report → DynamoDB → Amazon SNS → Admin Email. Backup: EventBridge Scheduler → SecureTable-Backup → DynamoDB Export to S3 → Amazon S3 → S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. All resources are configured in Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1. The schedules use the Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh time zone.
1. Create an Amazon SNS Topic for Report Delivery We use Amazon SNS to send reports from Lambda to the administrator’s email address.
Open Amazon SNS → Topics → Create topic.
Select Type: Standard.
Enter Name: SecureTable-FinancialReports.
Keep the settings appropriate for the demo environment, then select Create topic.
Copy the Topic ARN. It has the following format:
arn:aws:sns:ap-southeast-1:<YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID>:SecureTable-FinancialReports Open the newly created topic → Create subscription. Select Protocol: Email, enter the email address that will receive reports in the Endpoint field, then select Create subscription. Check your inbox, open the confirmation email from AWS, and select Confirm subscription. Return to SNS and verify that the subscription status is Confirmed. Note: If the subscription remains in the Pending confirmation state, SNS will not send reports to that email address. You can use Publish message in the SNS Topic to verify email delivery before connecting Lambda.
2. Configure and Test the Report Lambda The SecureTable-Report Lambda reads data from the business-related DynamoDB tables, generates reports, and sends their contents through SNS. The SecureTable-ReportDispatch table tracks report delivery status and helps prevent duplicate reports.
2.1. Configure the Report Lambda Open AWS Lambda → Functions → SecureTable-Report.
Select Configuration → Environment variables → Edit.
Add the following environment variable:
Key Value SNS_TOPIC_ARN The ARN of the SecureTable-FinancialReports topic created in Step 1 Select Save.
2.2. Test Report Delivery In SecureTable-Report, open Test → Create new event.
Create a test event with dry_run enabled:
{ "report_type": "DAILY", "business_date": "2026-11-27", "dry_run": true } Select Test, then review the response and CloudWatch Logs to check the generated report data. Change business_date to an actual date for which the system has data.
After confirming that the results are valid and the email subscription has been confirmed, you can test actual report delivery by changing "dry_run": false.
Check the received email and the corresponding record in SecureTable-ReportDispatch.
Note: dry_run: true only tests report generation; it does not mean the report was successfully delivered. When performing an actual send, check the SNS response and the status in SecureTable-ReportDispatch. Avoid repeatedly sending reports for the same reporting period; the deduplication mechanism is designed to help prevent duplicates.
3. Create EventBridge Schedules for Daily and Weekly Reports We will create two schedules that both invoke SecureTable-Report: one daily and one weekly.
Open Amazon EventBridge → Scheduler → Create schedule.
Name the schedule SecureTable-Daily-EmailReport.
Select Recurring schedule and configure the following settings:
Setting Value Schedule type Cron-based schedule Cron expression cron(0 22 * * ? *) Time zone Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh Flexible time window Off Schedule state Enabled Under Target, select AWS Lambda → Invoke, then choose SecureTable-Report.
Configure the Input / Payload:
{ "report_type": "DAILY", "scheduled_at": "<aws.scheduler.scheduled-time>" } Under Execution role, select Create new role for this schedule so that EventBridge Scheduler can invoke SecureTable-Report using the lambda:InvokeFunction permission.
Complete the process by selecting Create schedule.
Create the second schedule with these settings:
Setting Value Name SecureTable-Weekly-EmailReport Cron expression cron(15 22 ? * SUN *) Time zone Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh Flexible time window Off Target SecureTable-Report Enter the payload for the weekly report:
{ "report_type": "WEEKLY", "scheduled_at": "<aws.scheduler.scheduled-time>" } Create an Execution Role for this schedule when prompted by the Console, then complete the setup.
Note: The string <aws.scheduler.scheduled-time> is a context attribute that EventBridge Scheduler replaces with the scheduled execution time. Although the schedule uses the Vietnam time zone, the timestamp passed in the payload may be in UTC; Lambda must convert it to the correct reporting date. The Scheduler Execution Role is different from the Lambda Execution Role: Scheduler needs permission to invoke Lambda, while Lambda needs permissions to read DynamoDB and publish messages to SNS.
4. Enable Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) for DynamoDB To export DynamoDB data to S3, we must enable Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) on the tables included in the backup scope.
Open Amazon DynamoDB → Tables. Select a table, for example SecureTable-Bills. Open Backups → Point-in-time recovery (PITR) and select Turn on. Save the configuration and verify that its status changes to Enabled. Repeat these steps for the following 13 tables: No. DynamoDB Table 1 SecureTable-Bills 2 SecureTable-Orders 3 SecureTable-OrderItems 4 SecureTable-Ingredients 5 SecureTable-InventoryReceipts 6 SecureTable-InventoryCorrections 7 SecureTable-InventoryMovements 8 SecureTable-FinanceLedger 9 SecureTable-InventoryCounts 10 SecureTable-AuditLogs 11 SecureTable-Tables 12 SecureTable-MenuItems 13 SecureTable-ReceiptCorrectionState Note: Not all 18 tables are exported by this backup schedule. Supporting tables such as GuestSessions, Idempotency, PendingByIngredient, ReportDispatch, and NotificationOutbox are excluded from the list of 13 tables. PITR incurs charges while enabled, even if no export has been performed. After enabling PITR for the first time, you may need to wait until the recovery window covers the point in time requested by the Backup Lambda.
5. Create an S3 Bucket and Configure a Lifecycle Rule for Glacier The Backup Lambda will instruct DynamoDB to export data to a separate S3 bucket, rather than the bucket hosting the frontend.
5.1. Create an S3 Bucket for Backups Open Amazon S3 → General purpose buckets → Create bucket. Select the Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1 Region. Enter a unique bucket name, such as <YOUR_BACKUP_BUCKET> (replace it with a valid name that is not already in use). Keep Block all public access enabled. Use the default SSE-S3 encryption, then select Create bucket. 5.2. Create an S3 Lifecycle Rule Open the newly created bucket → Management → Create lifecycle rule. Name the rule, for example SecureTable-ArchiveToGlacier. Limit its scope using Prefix: securetable/weekly/. Select Transition current versions of objects between storage classes. Configure the following settings: Setting Value Choose storage class transitions S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval Transition after 30 days Expire after 180 days Note: By default, new S3 Lifecycle Rules do not transition objects smaller than 128 KB to another storage class. Some manifest files generated by DynamoDB exports may fall below this threshold. S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval also has transition fees, retrieval charges, and a minimum billable storage duration.
6. Configure and Test the Backup Lambda Open AWS Lambda → Functions → SecureTable-Backup → Configuration → Environment variables → Edit.
Add or update the following variables:
Key Value BACKUP_BUCKET The actual S3 backup bucket name, without s3:// BACKUP_PREFIX securetable/weekly Open Configuration → General configuration and use Memory: 256 MB and Timeout: 120 seconds as initial settings.
Open Configuration → Permissions and verify that the Inline Policy for SecureTable-Backup was obtained from Lambda/Backup/SecureTable-Backup.json.
Verify that <YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID> and <YOUR_BACKUP_BUCKET> have been replaced in the JSON, and that the permissions cover exports for the correct 13 tables and writing objects under securetable/weekly/*.
6.1. Test Without Creating an Export Open Test → Create new event for the Backup Lambda.
Enter the following payload:
{ "dry_run": true, "backup_id": "demo-2026-11-28" } Select Test.
Verify that the result includes ready: true and table_count: 13. If ready: false, check the list of missing tables or tables that do not have PITR enabled.
6.2. Test an Actual Export Once all 13 tables are ready, you can test an actual export with the following payload:
{ "dry_run": false, "backup_id": "demo-2026-11-28" } The Backup Lambda will request a DynamoDB Export to S3 for each table. The expected initiation response includes mode: STARTED, exports_requested: 13, and the export_arn values.
Open DynamoDB → Exports to S3 to check the status of the export jobs.
Wait for each export to reach COMPLETED; if any export shows FAILED, inspect its error details and CloudWatch Logs.
Open S3 → backup bucket and find the data under the corresponding prefix:
securetable/weekly/demo-2026-11-28/<table-name>/AWSDynamoDB/... Open the export folders to inspect the manifest files and exported data.
7. Create an EventBridge Scheduler for Weekly Backups Open Amazon EventBridge → Scheduler → Create schedule.
Enter Name: SecureTable-Weekly-DynamoBackup.
Select Recurring schedule and configure the following settings:
Setting Value Cron expression cron(0 2 ? * SUN *) Time zone Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh Flexible time window Off Target AWS Lambda → SecureTable-Backup Schedule state Enabled Under Input / Payload, enter:
{ "scheduled_at": "<aws.scheduler.scheduled-time>" } Under Execution role, select Create new role for this schedule, allowing EventBridge Scheduler to invoke only the SecureTable-Backup Lambda.
Review the settings and select Create schedule.
With this schedule, the Backup Lambda runs at 02:00 on Sundays (Vietnam time). Lambda selects a point in time within the PITR recovery window before initiating the exports. The DynamoDB Export jobs continue running after Lambda finishes.
After completing these steps, SecureTable automatically delivers reports through SNS and periodically backs up 13 DynamoDB tables to Amazon S3. In the next section, 5.8 – Security Hardening & System Monitoring, we will review CloudWatch, error alarms, and additional security configurations.

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
This section captures my reflections and feedback after completing the three-month First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ Workforce Bootcamp) internship. It has been a rewarding journey that enabled me, as an Information Assurance student, to translate theoretical cybersecurity principles into hands-on cloud architecture and security engineering skills on AWS.
General Evaluation 1. Learning and Working Environment
The FCAJ environment is open, motivating, and well-structured. The curated lab library on awsstudygroup.com provides a clear progression from cloud fundamentals to advanced architectures, enabling interns to build disciplined daily self-study and hands-on lab habits.
2. Support from Mentors and the Admin Team
The mentors and program coordinators were consistently supportive and professional. Whenever I encountered challenges with VPC routing, hybrid DNS resolution, or IAM policy scoping, mentors guided me on how to inspect logs and analyze root causes rather than simply giving away the answer. Program schedules, guidelines, and evaluation criteria were also communicated clearly from Week 1.
3. Alignment with My Information Assurance Major
The program aligned exceptionally well with my Information Assurance curriculum at FPT University. Beyond mastering foundational cloud infrastructure (VPC, EC2, S3, RDS, Serverless), I gained hands-on experience implementing enterprise cloud security controls including IAM Least Privilege, SSM Session Manager, AWS PrivateLink / VPC Endpoints, AWS KMS, AWS WAF, CloudTrail, GuardDuty, and Security Hub.
4. Learning & Holistic Skill Development
In addition to technical AWS capabilities, the internship trained me to design systems using the AWS Well-Architected Framework, estimate and govern infrastructure budgets with the AWS Pricing Calculator, publish bilingual technical documentation using Git and Hugo, and maintain structured weekly engineering worklogs.
5. Community Culture & Knowledge Sharing
The “Learn and Share” culture of the First Cloud Journey community left the strongest impression on me. Writing technical blogs and documenting a complete hands-on Workshop not only solidified my own understanding, but also contributed practical documentation back to the student cloud community.
Summary Reflection Questions What was I most satisfied with during the internship?
Getting true hands-on practice on a live AWS account solving enterprise-grade architecture scenarios, alongside attending in-person technical workshops at the AWS Vietnam office (Bitexco Financial Tower) to learn directly from AWS Solutions Architects.
What could be improved for future cohorts?
Adding mid-term thematic peer-review or mini Tech Talk sessions grouped by focus track (e.g., Cloud Security, Serverless Backend, Data & GenAI) would give interns even more opportunities to exchange architectural feedback.
Would I recommend the FCAJ internship to peers?
Absolutely yes. For students majoring in Information Assurance, Software Engineering, or Information Systems who want a rigorous, practical foundation in cloud computing, FCAJ is one of the best programs to launch an AWS career.
Suggestions & Acknowledgments I hope the First Cloud AI Journey program continues expanding advanced hands-on tracks in Cloud Security, DevSecOps, and Generative AI Security (Amazon Bedrock Security).
I would like to express my sincere gratitude to the mentors, the FCAJ Admin team, and Amazon Web Services Viet Nam Company Limited for their dedicated guidance, support, and inspiration throughout this internship!
