title: Security Hardening & System Monitoring
content:
SecureTable uses CloudFront + S3, Cognito + IAM, API Gateway + Lambda, and DynamoDB. We will use AWS WAF, Amazon CloudWatch, Amazon SNS, and AWS CloudTrail to improve observability and issue detection.
1. Review Frontend and API Security 1.1. Check S3 and CloudFront Open Amazon S3 → Buckets and select the bucket hosting the SecureTable frontend. Under Permissions, confirm that Block all public access is enabled. Verify that the Bucket policy grants only the read permissions required by CloudFront through Origin Access Control (OAC); do not enable public read access with Principal: "*". Open CloudFront → Distributions → select the SecureTable distribution → Origins. Confirm that the S3 Origin uses OAC and that the API Gateway Origin points to the REST API’s execute-api domain. Under Behaviors, check the following settings: Behavior Origin Settings to verify Default (*) S3 Frontend Redirect HTTP to HTTPS, OAC on the S3 Origin /v1/* API Gateway Redirect HTTP to HTTPS, CachingDisabled, AllViewerExceptHostHeader Note: APIs handling Guest Sessions, orders, and staff data must not be cached by CloudFront. CloudFront delivers the frontend over HTTPS, but it does not replace authentication and authorization checks in the backend.
1.2. Check Authentication and Authorization Open Amazon Cognito → User pools → SecureTable-Staff. Verify that Self-registration is disabled if staff accounts are created only by administrators. Confirm the Cognito Groups used by the application: RECEPTION, KITCHEN, INVENTORY, and ADMIN. Open API Gateway → SecureTable-API → Resources and confirm that Staff Methods use SecureTableStaffAuthorizer. For Staff APIs using Cognito ID Tokens, leave Authorization Scopes empty. Verify that each Lambda function also checks cognito:groups before processing business operations. 2. Review IAM Permissions Following the Principle of Least Privilege Each SecureTable Lambda function has its own Execution Role and a function-specific Inline Policy.
Open AWS Lambda → Functions and select a function, such as SecureTable-Ordering. Select Configuration → Permissions, then click the Execution Role name to open IAM. Confirm that the role has AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole for CloudWatch Logs and the correct function-specific Inline Policy. Compare the DynamoDB permissions against the tables that the Lambda function actually needs to access. Repeat these checks for important functions such as SecureTable-Kitchen, SecureTable-Report, and SecureTable-Backup. Lambda Permissions to review SecureTable-Ordering Read the menu, bills, and sessions; write orders and reserve ingredients SecureTable-Kitchen Read the queue; update item statuses, inventory, and bills SecureTable-AdminDashboard Read Finance data and Audit Logs SecureTable-Report Read reporting tables, update ReportDispatch, and call sns:Publish SecureTable-Backup Export 13 DynamoDB tables and write objects to the backup bucket Special check for the Backup Lambda: The S3 path in the IAM Policy must match the actual bucket and the BACKUP_PREFIX value configured in Section 5.7. For example, if the bucket is securetable-backup and the prefix is securetable/weekly, the object-write permission must cover:
arn:aws:s3:::securetable-backup/securetable/weekly/* The corresponding Inline Policy may need permissions including s3:PutObject, s3:PutObjectAcl, and s3:AbortMultipartUpload. Without s3:PutObject, Lambda may successfully initiate export requests, while the DynamoDB Export jobs still transition to FAILED due to AccessDenied.
3. Check AWS WAF on CloudFront Open CloudFront → Distributions → select the SecureTable distribution. Check Security / AWS WAF to identify the associated Web ACL (protection pack). Follow the link to AWS WAF and select the CloudFront distributions (Global) scope. Open the corresponding Web ACL and review Traffic overview, active rules, and the number of Allowed, Blocked, or Counted requests. If you add AWS Managed Rules or a Rate-based Rule, consider monitoring in Count mode first before switching to Block, to avoid accidentally blocking legitimate ordering or sign-in requests. Note: For a Web ACL protecting CloudFront, AWS WAF uses the Global / CloudFront scope (the API for managing these resources uses us-east-1), even though SecureTable’s Lambda functions and DynamoDB tables are hosted in Singapore. Check feature limits and costs under the current CloudFront Plan before enabling additional paid rules.
Protection limitation: A WAF associated with CloudFront inspects only requests that pass through CloudFront. If API Gateway’s default execute-api endpoint remains directly accessible, requests sent directly to that endpoint bypass the CloudFront Web ACL. Therefore, keep the Cognito Authorizer, Guest Token validation, and Lambda role checks in place.
4. Monitor AWS Lambda with CloudWatch 4.1. Check Log Groups AWS Lambda writes logs to CloudWatch when its Execution Role has the appropriate permissions. We will check logs for all 8 Lambda functions:
Open Amazon CloudWatch → Logs → Log Management in Region ap-southeast-1. Find log groups named /aws/lambda/SecureTable-.... Open /aws/lambda/SecureTable-Ordering or /aws/lambda/SecureTable-Kitchen. Select the most recent Log stream to inspect execution times, errors, and request-processing details. For each log group, select Actions → Edit retention setting, set a retention period such as 14 days for the demo environment, and save. 4.2. Check Metrics In AWS Lambda, open SecureTable-Ordering → Monitor → Metrics. Review the following metrics: Invocations, Errors, Duration, and Throttles. Repeat for SecureTable-Kitchen, SecureTable-Inventory, SecureTable-Report, and SecureTable-Backup. Metric Meaning Invocations Number of times the Lambda function is invoked Errors Number of executions that fail at the Lambda/runtime level Duration Function execution time Throttles Number of invocation requests rejected due to concurrency limits Note: If a Lambda function handles an error internally and returns JSON with HTTP 400 or 500 without an execution failure, the Lambda Errors metric may not increase. Therefore, combine Lambda metrics with API Gateway error metrics and application logs rather than relying on a single metric.
5. Enable Access Logging for the API Gateway REST API Access Logs help monitor requests to SecureTable-API, including requests rejected at the API Gateway layer.
5.1. Prepare CloudWatch Logs Permissions Open IAM → Roles and check whether a role for API Gateway to write CloudWatch Logs already exists. If none exists, create an IAM Role with Trusted entity: API Gateway (apigateway.amazonaws.com) and attach the AWS Managed Policy AmazonAPIGatewayPushToCloudWatchLogs. Copy the role’s ARN. Open API Gateway → Settings / Account settings in the Singapore Region and set CloudWatch log role ARN to the ARN of that role. Note: This is a role for API Gateway logging, separate from the Lambda Execution Roles and EventBridge Scheduler Execution Roles. Do not use a Lambda role for this step.
5.2. Configure Access Logging for the dev Stage Open API Gateway → APIs → SecureTable-API → Stages → dev.
Open Logs and tracing / Logging and enable Access logging.
Create or select a CloudWatch Log Group, for example /aws/apigateway/SecureTable-API-dev-access.
Enter the following JSON format for Access Logs:
{ "requestId": "$context.requestId", "requestTime": "$context.requestTime", "httpMethod": "$context.httpMethod", "resourcePath": "$context.resourcePath", "status": "$context.status", "responseLatency": "$context.responseLatency" } Save the configuration. In CloudWatch, set Log retention: 14 days for this log group if appropriate.
Call a valid API endpoint through CloudFront, then open the log group to confirm that new requests are being recorded.
Note: Log only the fields needed for monitoring. Do not include the Authorization header or request bodies containing session information in Access Logs. If you also enable Execution Logging, avoid enabling Data tracing in an environment with real data, as it may record sensitive request/response content and increase costs.
6. Create CloudWatch Alarms and SNS Notifications We will create an alarm for Lambda execution errors, using SecureTable-Ordering as an example. Other functions can be configured in the same way.
6.1. Create an SNS Topic for System Alerts Open Amazon SNS → Topics → Create topic. Select Standard and enter the name SecureTable-SystemAlerts. After creating the topic, select Create subscription with Protocol: Email. Enter the alert recipient’s email address and Confirm subscription from the inbox. 6.2. Create an Alarm for the Ordering Lambda Open CloudWatch → Alarms → All alarms → Create alarm.
Select Select metric → Lambda → By Function Name.
Select SecureTable-Ordering → the Errors metric.
Configure the following settings:
Setting Suggested value Statistic Sum Period 5 minutes Threshold type Static Condition Errors >= 1 Evaluation periods 1 Missing data treatment Treat missing data as not breaching Alarm action Send to SecureTable-SystemAlerts Alarm name SecureTable-Ordering-Errors Select Create alarm and confirm that it appears in the alarm list.
You can also create a similar alarm named SecureTable-Kitchen-Errors for the Kitchen Lambda.
Note: A threshold of Errors >= 1 over 5 minutes may generate too many alerts as the system grows. CloudWatch sends an SNS notification when the alarm changes to the relevant state, not one email for every failed request. Check both Alarm history and the confirmed email subscription to verify that alerts are working.
6.3. Monitor API Gateway Errors and Automated Tasks API Gateway: Open CloudWatch → Metrics → API Gateway or the Metrics page for SecureTable-API/dev. Review 4XXError, 5XXError, Count, and Latency. You can create an alarm for 5XXError if needed. 4XXError can also include legitimately rejected requests and does not necessarily indicate a system failure. Report Lambda: Check CloudWatch Logs, SNS Subscription status, and records in SecureTable-ReportDispatch to determine whether reports have been delivered. Backup Lambda: After running the function, always check DynamoDB → Exports to S3 until every job reaches COMPLETED. A successful Lambda execution does not mean an export has finished; S3 write errors such as AccessDenied may only appear during the export job. 7. Review AWS CloudTrail and Audit Logs AWS CloudTrail tracks management activity in AWS, while SecureTable Audit Logs record business-related changes in the application. These serve different purposes.
Open AWS CloudTrail → Event history in Region ap-southeast-1. Filter by Event name or Event source to find recent management actions involving Lambda, IAM, DynamoDB, or S3. Open an event to view its Event time, Event name, User name, and related details. Return to SecureTable, sign in as Admin, and open the Audit Dashboard. Compare business operations performed in the application, such as stock receipts, adjustments, or bill processing (if the application code records audit entries for those operations). Note: CloudTrail Event history shows management events from the last 90 days and does not replace business Audit Logs. Event history does not display data events such as every read or write of a DynamoDB item. To retain longer histories or record data events, configure an appropriate Trail or CloudTrail Lake setup and consider the associated costs.
8. Verify the Results After completing the steps, verify the following components:
Component Expected result S3 + CloudFront Bucket is not public; OAC and HTTPS work; API behavior does not cache responses Cognito + API Gateway Staff APIs require valid tokens; Lambda checks groups IAM All 8 Lambda functions have least-privilege, function-specific permissions; Backup has the correct S3 write permissions AWS WAF The Web ACL is associated with the correct CloudFront distribution and has observable metrics CloudWatch Logs New logs appear for Lambda functions and API Gateway Access Logs CloudWatch Alarm SecureTable-Ordering-Errors has been created and is linked to a confirmed SNS Topic CloudTrail Management events related to AWS resources can be viewed Backup Export jobs reach COMPLETED, rather than stopping at Lambda’s STARTED response Once these steps are complete, SecureTable can review and restrict access permissions, observe logs and metrics, receive execution-error alerts, and compare AWS management activity with business-level audit history.

title: End-to-End System Testing
content:
After completing the main components of SecureTable, we will test several business workflows to verify that CloudFront, Cognito, API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB work together. We will also test the automation features and the system’s observability.
1. Test the Frontend and Authentication Open https://<cloudfront-domain>/ to verify that the website is delivered through CloudFront from S3. Open the Staff login page and sign in with an Amazon Cognito account belonging to the RECEPTION or KITCHEN group. Confirm that the system redirects you to the appropriate interface. Try calling a Staff API without a valid token; the request should be rejected. Then try accessing a function outside the signed-in account’s permissions to verify authorization checks in Lambda. Expected result: The website loads over HTTPS; Staff can sign in; API Gateway validates the token, and Lambda checks cognito:groups before allowing business operations.
2. Test the Ordering Workflow: Customer → Kitchen → Billing On the Reception interface, select table T01 and open a bill. Before opening the bill, scan T01’s QR code to confirm that the Customer cannot place orders. Scan the QR code after the bill has been opened, select a dish, and click Send to Kitchen. The system calls POST /v1/guest/orders through CloudFront → API Gateway → Ordering Lambda. Open DynamoDB and check the new records in SecureTable-Orders and SecureTable-OrderItems, as well as the reserved ingredient quantities. Switch to the Kitchen interface and select Complete or Reject for the newly placed item. Return to the Customer page and open Ordered Items to check its updated status. On the Reception interface, close the bill and try placing another order using the old Guest Session. The system must reject requests associated with a closed bill. Expected result: Orders flow from Customer to Kitchen, item statuses are updated in DynamoDB, ingredient quantities are handled according to whether an item is completed or rejected, and the bill cannot receive additional orders after being closed.
3. Test Inventory, Automation, and Monitoring Sign in to the Inventory interface and create an ingredient purchase receipt. Check that the inventory quantity changes and confirm that a related entry appears in the Audit Dashboard, if that operation is recorded in the audit logs. Open Lambda SecureTable-Report and wait for the scheduled time configured in EventBridge. Verify that the report email has been successfully delivered to the Admin’s email account. Open Lambda SecureTable-Backup and run a dry_run test to verify the backup prerequisites for the 13 DynamoDB tables. For an export initiated earlier, open DynamoDB → Exports to S3 to confirm that its status is COMPLETED, then inspect the exported data in S3. Open CloudWatch Logs for the Lambda function that was executed and CloudTrail Event history to review the corresponding execution information and AWS management activities. After completing these tests, we can confirm that the main SecureTable workflows have been connected and tested across the user interface, APIs, database, and automation services.

title: Week 9 Worklog
content: Week 9 Objectives Implement a centralized API communication layer (apiClient.js) in the SecureTable Frontend aligned with the team’s Amazon API Gateway contract. title: Resource Cleanup
content:
After completing and testing SecureTable, we will delete AWS resources that are no longer needed to avoid unnecessary charges. All steps will be performed in the AWS Management Console. Most resources are located in Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1; CloudFront and AWS WAF for CloudFront are managed globally.
Note: The following actions may result in permanent data loss.
1. Stop Automated Schedules To prevent the Report Lambda from continuing to send emails and the Backup Lambda from starting additional export jobs, we will stop EventBridge Scheduler first.
Open Amazon EventBridge → Scheduler → Schedules in Region ap-southeast-1.
Find the following schedules:
Schedule Purpose SecureTable-Daily-EmailReport Send daily financial reports SecureTable-Weekly-EmailReport Send weekly financial reports SecureTable-Weekly-DynamoBackup Back up DynamoDB weekly Select each schedule and choose Disable if you want to pause it temporarily for verification. Then choose Delete when you are ready to clean up.
Check the schedule list again to confirm that no SecureTable schedules remain.
Note: Deleting a schedule does not automatically delete its Lambda function or the IAM Execution Role previously used by the Scheduler. We will review those roles in Section 7. If a DynamoDB export job has already been started, deleting the schedule will not automatically cancel that export.
2. Delete the CloudFront Distribution and AWS WAF Open Amazon CloudFront → Distributions and select the distribution serving the SecureTable website. If the distribution is using the CloudFront Free Plan or another Pricing Plan, select Cancel pricing plan first. For the Free Plan, cancellation usually takes effect immediately; for paid plans, you may need to wait until the end of the billing cycle. Choose Disable for the distribution and wait for the change to finish deploying. Once the distribution is disabled and is no longer associated with a pricing plan, choose Delete. Open AWS WAF → Web ACLs, select the CloudFront distributions (Global) scope, and check the SecureTable Web ACL. If the Web ACL is no longer used, delete it if it was not automatically removed along with the distribution. 3. Delete API Gateway, Lambda, and Cognito 3.1. Delete the REST API Open Amazon API Gateway → APIs in ap-southeast-1. Select SecureTable-API → Delete API, and confirm. Verify that the API and its dev stage no longer appear in the list. 3.2. Delete the Eight Lambda Functions Open AWS Lambda → Functions.
Select and delete each SecureTable function:
Lambda Function Lambda Function SecureTable-GuestServices SecureTable-Ordering SecureTable-Reception SecureTable-Kitchen SecureTable-Inventory SecureTable-AdminDashboard SecureTable-Report SecureTable-Backup Confirm that the functions no longer appear in the list.
3.3. Delete the Cognito User Pool Open Amazon Cognito → User pools. Select SecureTable-Staff and choose Delete user pool. If Deletion protection is enabled, follow the Console instructions to disable it before confirming deletion. 4. Delete the Amazon DynamoDB Tables Open Amazon DynamoDB → Tables in ap-southeast-1. Filter the list by SecureTable- and review the tables associated with the system. Select each table → Delete, and confirm as prompted by the Console. Continue until no SecureTable-* tables belonging to the project remain. The tables created in this workshop include:
SecureTable-Tables SecureTable-Bills SecureTable-Orders SecureTable-OrderItems SecureTable-MenuItems SecureTable-Ingredients SecureTable-InventoryReceipts SecureTable-InventoryCorrections SecureTable-ReceiptCorrectionState SecureTable-InventoryMovements SecureTable-InventoryCounts SecureTable-FinanceLedger SecureTable-AuditLogs SecureTable-GuestSessions SecureTable-Idempotency SecureTable-PendingByIngredient SecureTable-NotificationOutbox SecureTable-ReportDispatch Note: Deleting a table also deletes its active data. If you still need the data for demonstrations or verification, keep an appropriate backup before deleting it. Exports already stored in S3 are not automatically deleted when a DynamoDB table is deleted.
5. Delete the SecureTable S3 Buckets After CloudFront has been deleted and no export jobs are still writing to S3:
Open Amazon S3 → General purpose buckets. Select the frontend bucket created in Section 5.3 → Empty to remove the website files. Once the bucket is empty, choose Delete bucket and confirm. Repeat the process for the backup bucket created in Section 5.7 (for example, securetable-backup) if you no longer need the backups. Review the bucket list to confirm that both project buckets have been removed. Note: If S3 Versioning is enabled, you must also delete all object versions and delete markers. Objects transitioned to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval have a 90-day minimum billable storage duration; deleting them early may still incur storage charges for the remaining period. Only delete backups when you are certain that you will not need to restore the data.
6. Clean Up CloudWatch and SNS Open Amazon CloudWatch → Alarms → All alarms and delete the alarms created for SecureTable, such as SecureTable-Ordering-Errors and SecureTable-Kitchen-Errors. Open CloudWatch → Logs → Log groups and delete any log groups you no longer need, including /aws/lambda/SecureTable-* and /aws/apigateway/SecureTable-API-dev-access. Open Amazon SNS → Topics and delete the topics used only by this system: SecureTable-FinancialReports SecureTable-SystemAlerts Verify that the related subscriptions are no longer needed. Note: CloudWatch Logs may continue retaining data and incurring charges after a Lambda function has been deleted. CloudTrail Event history does not need to be deleted by default. If you created a dedicated CloudTrail Trail for SecureTable, delete it only after confirming that it is not shared with other resources; any log files stored in S3 and associated Log Groups must still be cleaned up separately.
7. Review IAM and Remaining Costs Open IAM → Roles and look for Execution Roles used exclusively by the eight SecureTable Lambda functions, the three EventBridge Schedules, and API Gateway Access Logging. Delete customer-created roles that are no longer in use. If a role has Inline Policies or attached Managed Policies, follow the Console instructions to remove those permissions before deleting the role. Do not delete shared AWS Managed Policies or service-linked roles. Review the resource lists in CloudFront, S3, Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB, Cognito, EventBridge Scheduler, SNS, and CloudWatch. Open Billing and Cost Management → Bills / Cost Explorer to monitor charges after cleanup. Cost data may be delayed, and charges incurred before cleanup will still appear. Result: The resources used by SecureTable have been stopped and deleted in the appropriate order, including automated schedules, the website, APIs, Lambda functions, databases, backups, monitoring resources, and IAM Roles that are no longer required.
